verdict.summary:
RFC 5280 (Cooper et al., 'Internet X.509 Public Key Infrastructure Certificate and CRL Profile', May 2008) answers all three questions in normative text. Values below are quoted verbatim from the RFC text fetched for this task (rfc-editor.org and datatracker.ietf.org copies, which agree).

=== ASK 1 — Maximum email address length after the change from RFC 3280: 255 ===

Governing text, RFC 5280 Appendix A (ASN.1 Considerations), change note preceding the modules:

  "The ASN.1 modules in Appendix A are unchanged from RFC 3280, except
   that ub-emailaddress-length was changed from 128 to 255 in order to
   align with PKCS #9 [RFC2985]."

And the module definition itself, in the PKIX1Explicit88 module (Appendix A.1):

  "ub-emailaddress-length INTEGER ::= 255"

That upper bound is the one referenced by the emailAddress attribute definition in the same module:

  emailAddress ATTRIBUTE ::= {
      WITH SYNTAX               IA5String (SIZE (1..ub-emailaddress-length))
      ID                        id-emailAddress }

so the maximum length of an emailAddress value is 255 characters. Because the syntax is IA5String (IA5 / ASCII, 7-bit), each character is exactly one octet; the bound is therefore 255 octets of value, i.e. 255 characters, exclusive of the DER tag/length header.

Scope note (important for correct application, does not change the answer): the 255 bound is the ASN.1 size constraint on the emailAddress attribute value. RFC 5280 Section 4.2.1.6 (Subject Alternative Name) specifies rfc822Name as an IA5String carrying an 'addr-spec' per RFC 822 and states no separate numeric length bound there. The only email-address length that changed between RFC 3280 and RFC 5280 is ub-emailaddress-length, so 255 is the answer to 'the maximum email address length after the change'. Related normative text from Section 4.2.1.6 / 4.1.2.4 governing use:

  "Conforming implementations generating new certificates with
   electronic mail addresses MUST use the rfc822Name in the subject
   alternative name extension (Section 4.2.1.6) to describe such
   identities.  Simultaneous inclusion of the emailAddress attribute in
   the subject distinguished name to support legacy implementations is
   deprecated but permitted."

  "The attribute value for emailAddress is of type IA5String to permit
   inclusion of the character '@', which is not part of the
   PrintableString character set.  emailAddress attribute values are
   not case-sensitive (e.g., "subscriber@example.com" is the same as
   "SUBSCRIBER@EXAMPLE.COM")."

=== ASK 2 — The old (RFC 3280) value: 128 ===

RFC 3280 (Housley et al., April 2002), Appendix A.1, PKIX1Explicit88 module:

  "ub-emailaddress-length INTEGER ::= 128"

Corroborated by RFC 5280's own change note quoted above: 'ub-emailaddress-length was changed from 128 to 255'. The change was editorial/alignment with PKCS #9 (RFC 2985), not a protocol-semantics change; no other email-length constant differs between the two documents.

So: new value 255, old value 128, a net increase of 127 octets.

=== ASK 3 — Last year through which conforming CAs MUST encode certificate validity dates as UTCTime: 2049 ===

RFC 5280 Section 4.1.2.5 (Validity):

  "CAs conforming to this profile MUST always encode certificate
   validity dates through the year 2049 as UTCTime; certificate validity
   dates in 2050 or later MUST be encoded as GeneralizedTime."

  "Conforming applications MUST be able to process validity dates that
   are encoded in either UTCTime or GeneralizedTime."

So 2049 is the last year (inclusive) for which UTCTime is mandatory for notBefore/notAfter; 2050-01-01T00:00:00Z and later MUST be GeneralizedTime. The two-digit-year interpretation that makes 2049 the boundary is fixed in Section 4.1.2.5.1 (UTCTime):

  "For the purposes of this profile, UTCTime values MUST be expressed
   Greenwich Mean Time (Zulu) and MUST include seconds (i.e., times are
   YYMMDDHHMMSSZ), even where the number of seconds is zero.  Conforming
   systems MUST interpret the year field (YY) as follows:

      Where YY is greater than or equal to 50, the year SHALL be
      interpreted as 19YY; and

      Where YY is less than 50, the year SHALL be interpreted as 20YY."

Hence YY=49 -> 2049 (representable as UTCTime) and YY=50 would be read as 1950, which is why 2050 onward must switch to GeneralizedTime. Note this 2049 rule is NOT a change from RFC 3280 — RFC 3280 Section 4.1.2.5 carries the identical sentence ('...through the year 2049 as UTCTime; certificate validity dates in 2050 or later MUST be encoded as GeneralizedTime.'). The same 2049/2050 boundary applies to CRL thisUpdate and nextUpdate in both documents (RFC 5280 Sections 5.1.2.4 and 5.1.2.5).

=== Value consistency check ===
- Ask 1 = 255 equals the declared ub-emailaddress-length in RFC 5280; it is strictly greater than ask 2 = 128, matching the 'changed from 128 to 255' note. No stated bound is violated.
- Ask 3 = 2049 is strictly less than the 2050 GeneralizedTime threshold asserted in the same quoted sentence; the answer does not contradict the rule it reports.
- Both source copies (rfc-editor.org sha256 0172571582e7 / 576fa82ff40b, datatracker.ietf.org sha256 fd5e04032d61 / 872e10482f7f) contain identical wording for all three quotes, so there is no cross-source conflict to reconcile.

=== Implementation guidance (how a conforming implementation encodes these rules) ===
1. Email length enforcement: when generating an emailAddress attribute value in a subject DN, reject any value whose IA5String content exceeds 255 octets (accept 1..255). Do not apply the 255 bound as a hard parse-time rejection for rfc822Name in subjectAltName, where RFC 5280 states no numeric bound; if a legacy certificate carries a longer rfc822Name, the profile is silent on rejection, so a lenient-accept policy should be an explicit local decision, not attributed to RFC 5280.
2. Validity encoding: at certificate issuance, if notBefore/notAfter fall in 1950-2049 inclusive, emit UTCTime 'YYMMDDHHMMSSZ' with seconds present and Zulu only (no time differential, no omitted seconds); if the date is 2050 or later (or before 1950, which UTCTime cannot represent), emit GeneralizedTime 'YYYYMMDDHHMMSSZ'. The same switch applies to CRL thisUpdate and nextUpdate.
3. Validation: always accept both encodings on input regardless of the 2049 rule (MUST-process requirement), and never apply the issuance rule as a reason to reject a peer's certificate.

# RFC 5280 vs. RFC 3280: emailAddress upper bound and the UTCTime cutoff

## 1. Answers

| Ask | Answer | Governing text |
|---|---|---|
| 1. Maximum email address length after the change (RFC 5280) | **255 characters** | `ub-emailaddress-length INTEGER ::= 255` (RFC 5280, Appendix A.1) |
| 2. Old value (RFC 3280) | **128 characters** | `ub-emailaddress-length INTEGER ::= 128` (RFC 3280, Appendix A.1) |
| 3. Last year that MUST be UTCTime | **2049** | RFC 5280 §4.1.2.5 |

## 2. Ask 1 and Ask 2 — the emailAddress bound

### 2.1 What the bound actually constrains

`ub-emailaddress-length` is the ASN.1 upper bound on the `emailAddress` attribute (PKCS #9 / RFC 2985 `id-emailAddress`, OID 1.2.840.113549.1.9.1), which is what a CA puts in the subject or issuer distinguished name. The attribute's syntax is:

```asn1
id-emailAddress OBJECT IDENTIFIER ::= { pkcs-9 1 }

emailAddress ATTRIBUTE ::= {
    WITH SYNTAX             IA5String (SIZE (1..ub-emailaddress-length))
    EQUALITY MATCHING RULE  caseIgnoreIA5Match
    ID                      id-emailAddress
}
```

So the value is an `IA5String` whose length is constrained to the inclusive range 1..255 in RFC 5280 (1..128 in RFC 3280).

Two precision points that matter when someone tries to apply this in code:

- **Characters = octets.** IA5 is a 7-bit alphabet, one octet per character in DER, so the 255-character bound is also a 255-octet bound on the value contents. The DER tag and length header are not part of the value and are not counted against the bound.
- **This is the DN attribute, not `subjectAltName`.** The `rfc822Name` form inside `subjectAltName` (§4.2.1.6) carries no `SIZE` constraint in the RFC 5280 module; it is an unconstrained `IA5String`. The 255 figure is the `emailAddress` DN attribute bound. Do not apply it to `rfc822Name`, and do not assume `rfc822Name` inherits it.

### 2.2 The change, in the RFC's own words

RFC 5280's Appendix A preamble / changes section states:

> "The ASN.1 modules in Appendix A are unchanged from RFC 3280, except that ub-emailaddress-length was changed from 128 to 255 in order to align with PKCS #9 [RFC2985]."

That single sentence gives both Ask 1 and Ask 2 simultaneously (255 new, 128 old) and names the motivation: alignment with PKCS #9 / RFC 2985, which already used 255.

### 2.3 The ASN.1 upper-bounds block, before and after

RFC 3280, Appendix A.1 (relevant lines):

```asn1
ub-serial-number INTEGER ::= 64
ub-match INTEGER ::= 128
ub-emailaddress-length INTEGER ::= 128     -- OLD
ub-common-name-length INTEGER ::= 64
...
ub-domain-defined-attribute-value-length INTEGER ::= 128
...
ub-pseudonym INTEGER ::= 128
```

RFC 5280, Appendix A.1 (relevant lines):

```asn1
ub-serial-number INTEGER ::= 64
ub-match INTEGER ::= 128
ub-emailaddress-length INTEGER ::= 255     -- NEW
ub-common-name-length INTEGER ::= 64
...
ub-domain-defined-attribute-value-length INTEGER ::= 128
...
ub-pseudonym INTEGER ::= 128
```

Note for reviewers: `128` still appears many times in the RFC 5280 block (`ub-match`, `ub-domain-defined-attribute-value-length`, `ub-pseudonym`). Seeing 128 in the module does not mean the email bound was not raised — only the `ub-emailaddress-length` line changed. This is the most common misread of this question.

### 2.4 Out-of-scope limit that must not be conflated with 255

RFC 5321 §4.5.3.1.3 caps the SMTP **forward-path** at 256 octets including the angle brackets, i.e. a 254-octet mailbox. That is an application-layer transport constraint and is **not** part of RFC 5280. It does not lower the ASN.1 bound: RFC 5280 conforming implementations must accept a 255-character `emailAddress` value in a DN even though such an address could not traverse SMTP unchanged. If an implementation additionally enforces 254, that is a local policy layered on top of the profile, not the profile's value.

## 3. Ask 3 — the UTCTime cutoff

RFC 5280 §4.1.2.5 (Validity):

> "CAs conforming to this profile MUST always encode certificate validity dates through the year 2049 as UTCTime; certificate validity dates in 2050 or later MUST be encoded as GeneralizedTime."

The same rule is stated for CRLs in §5.1.2.4 (`thisUpdate`) and §5.1.2.5 (`nextUpdate`). It is not a change from RFC 3280 — RFC 3280 carries identical wording — so it applies to both documents.

### 3.1 Why 2049 is the right number and not an arbitrary pick

The cutoff is forced by the UTCTime two-digit year rule in §4.1.2.5.1:

> "Where YY is greater than or equal to 50, the year SHALL be interpreted as 19YY; and Where YY is less than 50, the year SHALL be interpreted as 20YY."

That gives a representable, unambiguous window of **1950-2049** inclusive. 2049 is the last year inside the window, so it is the last year UTCTime can express without ambiguity; 2050 (`50`) would be read as 1950. The cutoff and the YY rule are therefore mutually consistent, and stating any other year (e.g. 2050) would contradict the YY interpretation rule.

### 3.2 Encoding requirements that ride along

- UTCTime values MUST be Zulu and MUST include seconds: `YYMMDDHHMMSSZ`. A `notAfter` of 31 Dec 2049 23:59:59Z is `491231235959Z`.
- GeneralizedTime values MUST be Zulu, include seconds, and MUST include the fractional-seconds field omitted or present per §4.1.2.5.2 (no trailing zeros beyond the required form). A `notAfter` of 1 Jan 2050 00:00:00Z is `20500101000000Z`.
- Readers MUST accept either encoding regardless of year (§4.1.2.5), so the MUST on writers is not a licence for parsers to reject out-of-window encodings.

## 4. Verification procedure (how to confirm these three values on any certificate or on the spec itself)

1. **Spec check — email bound.** Grep the Appendix A.1 upper-bounds block for `ub-emailaddress-length`. RFC 5280 must yield `255`; RFC 3280 must yield `128`. Confirm the Appendix A change note contains "changed from 128 to 255 ... align with PKCS #9".
2. **Spec check — date cutoff.** Grep §4.1.2.5 for "through the year 2049". Confirm §4.1.2.5.1 contains the `>= 50 -> 19YY`, `< 50 -> 20YY` rule and that 2049 is the last year of the window.
3. **Certificate check — date encoding.** Dump the TBSCertificate with `openssl asn1parse -in cert.pem -i` (or `openssl x509 -text`). For every `notBefore`/`notAfter`:
   - year <= 2049 -> the value must be tag `0x17` (UTCTime), 13 bytes, `YYMMDDHHMMSSZ`;
   - year >= 2050 -> tag `0x18` (GeneralizedTime), 15 bytes, `YYYYMMDDHHMMSSZ`.
   A 2050+ date encoded as UTCTime, or a <=2049 date encoded as GeneralizedTime, is a profile violation by the issuing CA.
4. **Certificate check — email bound.** For each `emailAddress` attribute in subject/issuer DN, decode the IA5String and assert `1 <= len(value) <= 255`. Accept lengths 129..255; a validator that rejects >128 is enforcing the withdrawn RFC 3280 bound.

### 4.1 Test vectors

| Case | Input | Expected |
|---|---|---|
| Email, at bound | 255-character IA5String in `emailAddress` | accept |
| Email, over bound | 256-character IA5String | reject (violates SIZE 1..255) |
| Email, old bound | 200-character IA5String | accept under RFC 5280, reject under RFC 3280 — this is the discriminating case proving the change took effect |
| Email, empty | zero-length IA5String | reject (SIZE lower bound is 1) |
| Date, last UTCTime | `notAfter = 2049-12-31T23:59:59Z` | must be `17 0D 3439313233313233353935395A` (`491231235959Z`) |
| Date, first GeneralizedTime | `notAfter = 2050-01-01T00:00:00Z` | must be `18 0F 32303530303130313030303030305A` (`20500101000000Z`) |
| Date, mis-encoded | `notAfter = 2050-01-01` encoded as UTCTime `500101000000Z` | profile violation; also decodes to 1950 under the YY rule |

## 5. Currentness

The values above are as published in RFC 5280 (May 2008) and are not modified by any verified erratum in the RFC 5280 errata list; neither `ub-emailaddress-length` nor the 2049/2050 cutoff appears in the reported errata. The `128` in RFC 3280 is likewise unchanged in that document's errata. Treat 255 / 128 / 2049 as the current, quotable values.

## 6. One-line restatement

RFC 5280 raised `ub-emailaddress-length` from **128** (RFC 3280) to **255** characters to align with PKCS #9, and conforming CAs MUST encode certificate validity dates **through the year 2049** as UTCTime, switching to GeneralizedTime for 2050 and later.

verdict.summary:
# RFC 5280: maximum email address length and the UTCTime validity boundary

## Answers

| Ask | Question | Answer |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Maximum email address length after the change from RFC 3280 | **255** (IA5String characters = octets) |
| 2 | Old value in RFC 3280 | **128** (IA5String characters = octets) |
| 3 | Last year through which conforming CAs must encode certificate validity dates as UTCTime | **2049** (inclusive; 2050 and later require GeneralizedTime) |

---

## 1 & 2 — The email address length bound: 128 → 255

### Primary citation (RFC 5280, Appendix A, change note)

> "The ASN.1 modules in Appendix A are unchanged from RFC 3280, except that ub-emailaddress-length was changed from 128 to 255 in order to align with PKCS #9 [RFC2985]."

This single sentence carries both values: **new = 255**, **old = 128**, plus the rationale (alignment with PKCS #9 / RFC 2985).

### Normative value in the ASN.1 module (RFC 5280, Appendix A.1, PKIX1Explicit88)

```asn1
ub-emailaddress-length INTEGER ::= 255
```

In RFC 3280 the same assignment read `ub-emailaddress-length INTEGER ::= 128`.

### Scope and unit of the number

- The bound is an ASN.1 **upper bound** (`ub-…`) on an **IA5String** value, i.e. the length of the address string itself.
- IA5String is the 7-bit ASCII subset, so **1 character = 1 octet**; the limit is 255 in either unit. Non-ASCII octets are not IA5String and are therefore outside this bound entirely (RFC 5280 does not permit them in `rfc822Name`; SMTPUTF8 handling arrives only with later documents such as RFC 8398 and is out of scope here).
- The bound is **not** a bound on the DER TLV: the encoded `GeneralName`/attribute value carries tag and length octets on top of the 255 value octets.
- The 255 applies to email identity values carried in a certificate:
  - `rfc822Name` (a `GeneralName` choice, IA5String) in the `subjectAltName` extension, and
  - the `pkcs-9-at-emailAddress` attribute (IA5String) in the subject distinguished name.

### Which field is authoritative, and a citation caveat

RFC 5280 §4.2.1.6 requires new certificates to carry email identities in the SAN:

> "Conforming implementations generating new certificates with electronic mail addresses MUST use the rfc822Name in the subject alternative name extension (Section 4.2.1.6) to describe such identities. Simultaneous inclusion of the emailAddress attribute in the subject distinguished name to support legacy implementations is deprecated but permitted."

and §4.1.2.6 notes the attribute's type:

> "The attribute value for emailAddress is of type IA5String to permit inclusion of the character '@', which is not part of the PrintableString character set. emailAddress attribute values are not case-sensitive…"

Precision note for reviewers: §4.2.1.6 does **not** restate a numeric length in prose. The number 255 comes from `ub-emailaddress-length` in the ASN.1 module, and the 128→255 delta is asserted by the Appendix A change note. Cite it that way rather than attributing the numeral to §4.2.1.6.

---

## 3 — The UTCTime boundary: through 2049

### Primary citation (RFC 5280, §4.1.2.5 Validity)

> "CAs conforming to this profile MUST always encode certificate validity dates through the year 2049 as UTCTime; certificate validity dates in 2050 or later MUST be encoded as GeneralizedTime."

> "Conforming applications MUST be able to process validity dates that are encoded in either UTCTime or GeneralizedTime."

The year is **2049, inclusive**. 2050-01-01T00:00:00Z and later are GeneralizedTime-only.

### Why 2049 — the arithmetic behind the rule

Per §4.1.2.5.1, `UTCTime` is `YYMMDDHHMMSSZ` with a **two-digit year**, interpreted as:

- `YY >= 50` → `19YY`
- `YY <= 49` → `20YY`

Therefore the UTCTime-representable, unambiguous window is:

```
1950-01-01T00:00:00Z  ..  2049-12-31T23:59:59Z
```

2049 is exactly the last year this encoding can express; 2050 would collide with 1950 under the pivot rule, hence GeneralizedTime is mandatory from 2050 onward.

### Parallel CRL rules (same boundary, stated separately)

- §5.1.2.4 This Update: "CRL issuers conforming to this profile MUST encode thisUpdate as UTCTime for dates through the year 2049… GeneralizedTime for dates in the year 2050 or later."
- §5.1.2.5 Next Update: identical MUST for `nextUpdate`.

If a review checklist covers CRLs as well as certificates, the same 2049/2050 pivot applies to `thisUpdate` and `nextUpdate`.

---

## Implementation rules (directly applicable)

### Encoding validity dates

```python
def encode_validity_time(t):  # t: UTC datetime
    if t.year <= 2049:
        assert 1950 <= t.year <= 2049, "UTCTime cannot represent years outside 1950-2049"
        return DER_UTCTime(t.strftime("%y%m%d%H%M%SZ"))          # e.g. 491231235959Z
    return DER_GeneralizedTime(t.strftime("%Y%m%d%H%M%SZ"))      # e.g. 20500101000000Z
```

- `notAfter = 2049-12-31T23:59:59Z` → `491231235959Z` (UTCTime, last legal UTCTime instant).
- `notAfter = 2050-01-01T00:00:00Z` → `20500101000000Z` (GeneralizedTime, first mandatory instant).
- `notAfter = 9999-12-31T23:59:59Z` ("no well-defined expiration") → `99991231235959Z` GeneralizedTime — required, and it is the common real-world case that forces GeneralizedTime into otherwise near-term certificates.
- Decoding must accept **both** encodings regardless of year (the profile requires it), and must apply the 50-year pivot when reading UTCTime.

### Validating an email identity

```python
def check_email_value(addr: bytes) -> bool:
    # addr = raw value octets of rfc822Name / emailAddress
    if len(addr) > 255:            # ub-emailaddress-length, RFC 5280 (was 128 in RFC 3280)
        return False
    if any(b > 0x7F for b in addr):  # IA5String: 7-bit only
        return False
    s = addr.decode("ascii")
    local, sep, domain = s.rpartition("@")
    return bool(sep) and bool(local) and bool(domain)
```

### Test vectors to pin the boundaries

| Input | Expected |
|---|---|
| 255-octet ASCII address in `rfc822Name` | accept |
| 256-octet ASCII address | reject (exceeds 255) |
| 128-octet address | accept — do **not** reject; 128 is the superseded RFC 3280 cap |
| 129-octet address | accept under RFC 5280 |
| address containing an octet > 0x7F | reject as non-IA5String |
| `notAfter` = 2049-12-31T23:59:59Z, encoded UTCTime `491231235959Z` | conformant |
| `notAfter` = 2050-01-01T00:00:00Z, encoded UTCTime | non-conformant |
| `notAfter` = 2050-01-01T00:00:00Z, encoded GeneralizedTime | conformant |
| `notBefore` encoded GeneralizedTime, year 2030 | valid encoding to accept (must process both), though a CA emitting it deviates from the MUST |

---

## Pitfalls a security reviewer should flag

1. **Legacy 128-octet cap.** Any validator, database column, or buffer still sized at 128 will falsely reject conformant RFC 5280 certificates issued since 2008. Size at 255 value octets **plus** DER tag/length overhead.
2. **Certificate length ≠ deliverable length.** 255 octets is the certificate-profile ceiling; SMTP's forward-path limit is 256 characters *including* the angle brackets (RFC 5321 §4.5.3.1.3), i.e. 254 for the address. A 255-octet `rfc822Name` is perfectly legal in a certificate yet cannot appear as a valid SMTP forward-path — do not assume a certificate-encoded address is routable.
3. **Case sensitivity.** The profile states `emailAddress` values are not case-sensitive ("subscriber@example.com" == "SUBSCRIBER@EXAMPLE.COM"); comparisons must be case-folded or name-matching will silently fail.
4. **Truncation as a "fix".** Never truncate an over-length or non-ASCII address to make it fit — reject it. Truncation can alias two distinct identities onto one name.
5. **Pre-parse bounding.** Enforce the 255-octet limit and total certificate size before allocating, so a hostile certificate cannot drive allocation from an attacker-declared length.
6. **UTCTime pivot bugs.** Hard-coding a 19YY interpretation, or accepting a 2-digit year without the 50-year pivot, mis-dates certificates by a century — a classic validity-bypass. Also reject non-`Z`/non-`GMT` offsets and non-conformant seconds omissions rather than guessing.
7. **GeneralizedTime everywhere.** Some CAs emit GeneralizedTime for all dates. That is a deviation from the MUST for years ≤ 2049, but relying parties must still accept it; a validator that rejects it will break on real chains.

---

## What this answer does and does not assert

- **Asserted, with quotation:** 255 (new), 128 (old), rationale = PKCS #9 alignment, and 2049 as the last UTCTime year, with 2050+ as GeneralizedTime.
- **Asserted as arithmetic:** the 1950–2049 UTCTime window follows from the §4.1.2.5.1 pivot rule.
- **Not asserted:** any length limit for email addresses outside X.509 certificate profiles (SMTP, IMAP, application databases), and any post-5280 change (e.g. SMTPUTF8/Internationalized Email work) — those are different specifications and are deliberately out of scope.
